Here is the itemized extraction of Mireia Ryšková's positions and claims across the substantive B001 items (and their immediate contextual citation units) in her article, "The Reception of the Book of Isaiah in Paul's Letter to the Romans" (2019).
B001-4: Romans 10:11 / Isaiah 28:16 (and Romans 9:33)
S06F-E001
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E001
B001 Passage ID: B001-4
Author's Claim: In Romans 10:11, Paul quotes directly from LXX Isaiah 28:16 and adds the pronoun πᾶς ("no one / everyone") to emphasize the universal availability of salvation through faith in Christ.
Short Exact Quotation: "The universal aspect of the statement is emphasised by the pronoun ‘no one’ (πᾶς), which is missing from the quotation in Romans 9:33."
Printed Page Number: Page 104
NotebookLM Citation:
1
Textual Evidence Invoked: LXX rendering of Isaiah 28:16 vs. Hebrew MT; insertion of πᾶς in Rom 10:11 compared to Rom 9:33.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Textual-critical
Qualifications / Conditions: The pronoun πᾶς is absent from LXX Isaiah 28:16 and from Paul's earlier citation in Romans 9:33.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S06F-E002
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E002
B001 Passage ID: B001-4
Author's Claim: In Romans 10:11, Paul shifts the metaphorical context of the "stone" in Isaiah 28:16 from a judge (as in Rom 9:33) to the resurrection of Jesus Christ and faith in that resurrection.
Short Exact Quotation: "The stone is no longer a judge but the resurrection of Jesus Christ and faith in that resurrection."
Printed Page Number: Page 104
NotebookLM Citation:
1
Textual Evidence Invoked: Re-contextualization of Isaiah 28:16 in Rom 10:11 following its composite use in Rom 9:33.
Claim Type: Exegetical
Qualifications / Conditions: No one who believes in Jesus and professes Him as the resurrected Lord will be put to shame.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S06F-E003
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E003
B001 Passage ID: B001-4
Author's Claim: Paul applies Isaiah's monotheistic statements in Isaiah 28:16 (cited in Rom 9:33 and 10:11) to both God and Christ, presenting Christ as co-sovereign and co-unique with God the Father.
Short Exact Quotation: "Paul is applying Isaiah’s monotheistic statements both to God and to Christ, the Lord, who is co-sovereign and co-unique with God the Father."
Printed Page Number: Page 104
NotebookLM Citation:
2
Textual Evidence Invoked: Parallel citations of Isaiah 28:16 in Rom 9:33 and 10:11.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Theological
Qualifications / Conditions: Introductions to both citations rely on general references to "Scripture" rather than naming Isaiah directly.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S06F-E004
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E004
B001 Passage ID: B001-4
Author's Claim: In Romans 9:33, Paul merges Isaiah 28:16 and Isaiah 8:14 into a composite "stone" quotation to show that trusting in legalistic works caused Israel to stumble over Christ, while faith yields certainty.
Short Exact Quotation: "This verse is a composite of two passages from Isaiah with the common theme of ‘stone’..."
Printed Page Number: Page 103
NotebookLM Citation:
3
Textual Evidence Invoked: Conflation of Isa 28:16 and Isa 8:14 in Rom 9:33; comparison with 1 Pet 2:6–8.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Textual-critical
Qualifications / Conditions: Whether Paul relied on a pre-Pauline written/oral testimony tradition or quoted directly from an Isaiah scroll in Corinth is debated among scholars.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
B001-5: Romans 10:13 / Joel 2:32 [LXX 3:5] (Surrounding Context to B001-4)
S06F-E005
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E005
B001 Passage ID: B001-5
Author's Claim: The citation of Isaiah 28:16 in Romans 10:11 corresponds directly with the unmarked quotation of Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5) in Romans 10:13 to establish faith (πίστις) as the fundamental scriptural criterion for salvation.
Short Exact Quotation: "The verse from Isaiah corresponds to the unmarked quotation from Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5) in Romans 10:13."
Printed Page Number: Page 104
NotebookLM Citation:
2
Textual Evidence Invoked: Pairing of Rom 10:11 (Isa 28:16) and Rom 10:13 (Joel 3:5 LXX).
Claim Type: Exegetical / Literary
Qualifications / Conditions: The Joel passage is cited without an explicit introductory quotation formula.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
B001-6: Romans 11:34 / Isaiah 40:13
S06F-E006
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E006
B001 Passage ID: B001-6
Author's Claim: In Romans 11:34, Paul quotes almost word-for-word from LXX Isaiah 40:13 without an introductory formula, incorporating it into a hymn-like doxology expressing God's unsearchable sovereignty.
Short Exact Quotation: "Paul quotes here almost word for word from Isaiah 40:13... in a hymn-like doxology that expresses the greatness of God..."
Printed Page Number: Page 108
NotebookLM Citation:
4
Textual Evidence Invoked: Near-verbatim Greek agreement between Rom 11:34 and LXX Isa 40:13; pairing with Job 41:11 (LXX 41:3) in Rom 11:35.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Literary
Qualifications / Conditions: Paul quotes either from memory or by drawing on familiar biblical idiom without explicitly signaling a scriptural reference.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S06F-E007
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E007
B001 Passage ID: B001-6
Author's Claim: Paul adapts Isaiah 40:13 selectively according to his contextual purpose, omitting the end of the verse in Romans 11:35 while omitting its middle clause in 1 Corinthians 2:16.
Short Exact Quotation: "Elsewhere, in Romans 11:35, he omits the end of Isaiah 40:13; in 1 Corinthians 2:16, he leaves out the middle section."
Printed Page Number: Page 108
NotebookLM Citation:
4
Textual Evidence Invoked: Comparison of Rom 11:34–35 and 1 Cor 2:16 against LXX Isa 40:13.
Claim Type: Literary / Textual-critical
Qualifications / Conditions: Reflects Paul's ability to adapt scriptural passages at will to suit different epistolary contexts.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
B001-7: Romans 15:12 / Isaiah 11:10
S06F-E008
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E008
B001 Passage ID: B001-7
Author's Claim: In Romans 15:12, Paul places Isaiah 11:10 as the culmination of the citation chain in Romans 15:9–12, marking an ideological shift from general praise of God to the "root of Jesse" as the hope of the Gentiles.
Short Exact Quotation: "The quotations from Scripture culminate in the quotation from Isaiah 11:10, which is introduced by an explicit reference to the prophet."
Printed Page Number: Pages 109–110
NotebookLM Citation:
5
6
Textual Evidence Invoked: Citation chain of Ps 18:49, Deut 32:43, Ps 117:1, and Isa 11:10 in Rom 15:9–12; introductory formula Ἠσαΐας λέγει.
Claim Type: Exegetical / Structural
Qualifications / Conditions: Shifts focus from the internal community problem of the "weak and strong" to God's universal generosity in Christ.
Extraction Confidence: HIGH
S06F-E009
Proposed Evidence ID: S06F-E009
B001 Passage ID: B001-7
Author's Claim: Paul uses Isaiah 11:10 in Romans 15:12 to present Jesus Christ as the promised messianic ruler over the nations who unites Jewish and Gentile believers in shared praise.
Short Exact Quotation: "Jesus Christ is the promised shoot from the stump of Jesse, the Messiah, the sovereign Lord, the ruler over the nations and the hope of salvation for the Gentiles..."
Printed Page Number: Page 110
NotebookLM Citation:
6
Textual Evidence Invoked: LXX Isa 11:10 text cited in Rom 15:12 (ἔσται ἡ ῥίζα τοῦ Ἰεσσαί...).
Claim Type: Exegetical / Christological
Qualifications / Conditions: Serves as a positive motivation for Gentile believers to praise God while preparing for Paul's concluding travel plans (Rom 15:14–33).
Extraction Confidence: HIGH

Rom 10:11 (Is 28:16) Quoting directly from the LXX (which differs from the MT), Paul returns to Isaiah 28:16 to drive home his point that salvation comes through faith in God’s redeeming work in Christ. The quotation is used in a different context from 9:33. No one who believes in Jesus and pro- fesses him as the resurrected Lord will ever be put to shame. The stone is no longer a judge but the resurrection of Jesus Christ and faith in that resurrection. The universal aspect of the statement is emphasised by the pronoun ‘no one’ (πᾶς), which is missing from the quotation in Romans 9:33.

The quotation is used in a different context from 9:33. No one who believes in Jesus and pro- fesses him as the resurrected Lord will ever be put to shame. The stone is no longer a judge but the resurrection of Jesus Christ and faith in that resurrection. The universal aspect of the statement is emphasised by the pronoun ‘no one’ (πᾶς), which is missing from the quotation in Romans 9:33.

It is clear from both quotations that Paul is applying Isaiah’s mono- theistic statements both to God and to Christ, the Lord, who is co-sov- ereign and co-unique with God the Father. 40 This quotation, which like 9:33 is introduced by a general reference to Scripture, emphasises the role played by faith in God’s redeeming work accomplished in the res- urrection of Jesus. The verse from Isaiah corresponds to the unmarked quotation from Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5) in Romans 10:13. By repeating the reference to Isaiah 28:16, and ‘based on his commitment to the validity of the gospel for both Jew and Gentile’, 41 Paul is able to anchor in Scrip- ture his fundamental criterion, which is faith (πίστις).

5. Rom 9:33 (Is 28:16; 8:14) This verse is a composite of two passages from Isaiah with the com- mon theme of ‘stone’; a similar passage can be found in 1 Peter 2:6–8. Some scholars (Koch and Dodd, for example) believe that the combi- nation is a pre-Pauline tradition (Koch oral; Dodd written) 35 and that Paul is therefore quoting from Isaiah on the basis of an existing text; the quotation is introduced with the general ‘as it is written’. Shum is certain that Paul is quoting directly from a scroll of Isaiah he might have had access to in Corinth. 36 The passage concerns the rejection of human attempts to achieve their salvation without regard to God. It is not completely clear, however, if Isaiah’s stone was a reference to God or the temple: 37 in Isaiah 28:16, the prophet is speaking primarily about the foundation of a new temple; in 8:14 the ‘stone’ is the Lord God who dwells in the temple.

The verse from Isaiah corresponds to the unmarked quotation from Joel 2:32 (LXX 3:5) in Romans 10:13. By repeating the reference to Isaiah 28:16, and ‘based on his commitment to the validity of the gospel for both Jew and Gentile’, 41 Paul is able to anchor in Scrip- ture his fundamental criterion, which is faith (πίστις).

The final three – rhetorical – questions address the subject of God’s sovereignty. Without pointing it out, Paul quotes here almost word for word from Isaiah 40:13 – with a possible echo of Job 41:11 (LXX 41:3) – in a hymn-like doxology that expresses the greatness of God and the unsearchable nature of his ways. Paul is either quoting by heart from his great knowledge of Isaiah or using Isaiah’s language automatically, naturally. This ability to quote at will enables him to adapt Scriptures according his purpose. Elsewhere, in Romans 11:35, he omits the end of Isaiah 40:13; in 1 Corinthians 2:16, he leaves out the middle section.

59 Wilk, Die Bedeutung des Jesajabuches für Paulus, 389–390. intentionally ambiguous. 60 We find a wholly Christocentric appropria- tion of Isaiah 45:23b in Philippians 2:10–11. 14. Rom 15:12 (Is 11:10) This quotation from Isaiah follows the short series of quotations from the Psalms and Deuteronomy which begin in verse 9 and give praise to the Lord for his mercy. There is something of a discontinu- ity – an ideological shift – between the quotations from Psalms/Deu- teronomy and the verse from Isaiah. From explicit praise of the Lord, attention moves to the ‘root of Jesse’, who is the hope of the Gentiles. From a focus on the problem of the weak and the strong in the com- munity, Paul moves on to praise God’s generosity in Christ, who gave himself freely for all.

The quotations from Scripture culminate in the quotation from Isa- iah 11:10, which is introduced by an explicit reference to the prophet. Paul’s aim is to show his readers the greatness of God’s offer in Jesus, the pinnacle and model of God’s love, so that they may be moved to a similar generosity. God’s positive move towards his people presup- poses an appropriate response. The quotation from Isaiah seeks to em- phasise what the readers have received as Gentiles. The promise to Israel applies also to them, so they should behave towards each other in an appropriate manner. The quotations provide a positive motivation for Paul’s readers: Jesus Christ is the promised shoot from the stump of Jesse, the Messiah, the sovereign Lord, the ruler over the nations and the hope of salvation for the Gentiles; he is the Christ who ‘did not please himself’ (verse 3), who unites all people. The community should therefore come together in praise of God. Paul is also preparing the way for the conclusion to the letter in 15:14–33. 61
